To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) NOx and SO2 emissions from the petrochemical sources in Houston, TX, have decreased since 2000, (2) ethene (C2 H4) and propylene (C3H 6) are major contributors to ozone production, and (3) ethene and propylene emissions from isolated petrochemical plants in Houston have decreased since 1999. [2]

(1) the emission ratios of NOx and SO2 from petrochemical facilities in Houston have changed by −29% and 3% between 2000–2006, respectively; (2) ethene and propylene are emitted in large amounts and are the major contributors of hydrocarbon reactivity to ozone formation; (3) ethene and ethane emissions have decreased by 52% and 20% since 2000, respectively.

(i) ethene and propylene are the major contributors of ozone production from the petrochemical sources; (ii) the petrochemical facilities have high ethene and propylene emissions, and these have decreased between 2000–2006; and (iii) the petro-chemical facilities emit significant amounts of formaldehyde, acetylaldehyde and peroxyacetylnitrate.

the emission and photochemical processing of hydrocarbons in the urban atmosphere, and the results have implications for ozone production and the development of emission inventories. [1]
the characterization of industrial emissions of reactive hydrocarbons and NOx in Houston, Texas, and the implications of these emissions for regional air quality and ozone formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the petrochemical sources have reduced emissions of NOx and hydrocarbons between 2000 (TexAQS I) and 2006 (TexAQS-II), but the reduction in hydrocarbons has been less than the reduction in NOx, and thus the ozone formation potential has not changed.
NOx, SOx, and VOC emissions from petrochemical sources in Houston have not changed significantly between 2000–2006.
the petrochemical facilities are a significant source of ethene and a major source of propene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
emissions of ethene and other alkenes are significant and variable, and the emissions are not well characterized by current inventory estimates.

the petrochemical industry in Houston continues to be a major source of ozone precursors, and there are no indications of a decrease in emissions of ethene and other hydrocarbons between TexAQS I and TexAQS II.
the petrochemical sources in Houston are major emitters of NOx, C2H4, and C3H4, and these emissions are important in the rapid ozone production that is observed in Houston.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the petrochemical industry in Houston has made significant improvements to reduce hydrocarbon and NOx emissions, and the resulting ambient concentrations of ozone precursors have been reduced.
the petrochemical industry is a significant contributor to the urban air quality problem in Houston.
the petrochemical industry has reduced emissions of ethene and ozone-forming precursors in the past decade, and the reduction is reflected in the ambient ozone levels.
